summary.text: 字 is traditionally analyzed as 子 beneath 宀, with 子 also serving as a sound element. A Han-era lexicographic account associates it with birth or nurture; today it commonly means “written character.” The connection between these meanings remains unresolved.

formation.text: The traditional analysis is phonosemantic: 宀 depicts a roof or indoor setting, while 子 depicts a child and is assigned a sound role. The reported bronze-form account describes 子 below 宀, but the analysis has been challenged and the available evidence does not detail alternatives.

components.text: In the traditional child-under-a-roof interpretation, 宀 depicts a roof or indoor setting. This is a proposed reading of the graph, not an independently verified paleographic conclusion.
In the traditional interpretation, 子 depicts the child beneath the roof and is also assigned a phonetic role.

sound_limitation.text: The reported Old Chinese comparison is compatible with a sound role, but its exact dataset entries were not independently verified against the upstream dataset; the modern Mandarin pair alone does not establish the ancient relation.

sound.text: In the Baxter–Sagart local dataset notation, 子 is reported as *[ts]əʔ / *tsəʔ and 字 as *mə-dzə(ʔ)-s. Their consonant correspondences are compatible with 子 serving as a phonetic element, but the comparison does not by itself prove that graphic analysis.
Current Mandarin readings are 子 zǐ and 字 zì. This modern comparison does not establish the ancient sound relation.

history.text: A reported bronze-form account describes 子 below 宀. A catalog records a Shang-period rubbing associated with 字父己觶, but this does not establish the inscription’s reading in context or make it the earliest attestation.

The traditional construction has been challenged, but the available account of that disagreement does not provide enough detail to assess alternative readings. The evidence does not identify graphic corruption or miscopying.

uncertainties.text: The child-under-a-roof construction is a transmitted historical explanation, and the available evidence reports disagreement without enough detail to evaluate competing analyses.

senses.period: Han lexicographic account; earlier dating unresolved
senses.text: A Han lexicographic account gives birth or nurture as a meaning, but does not establish when either sense arose or whether the glosses represent one original lexical meaning.
字 commonly means a written character. The available material does not date the earliest use of this sense.
“Word” is also a recorded meaning; its chronology and relation to the birth or nurture sense are unresolved.

developments.text: A later commentary links birth to nurture and then to written characters; another account allows a distinct root or a derivation from producing or generating. The proposed relationship and its chronology remain unresolved.

limitations.text: Dictionary glosses and the Han-era explanation that written forms multiply do not independently establish the chronology or development of these meanings.

overview.text: 字 is traditionally explained as a child (子) beneath a roof (宀), with 子 also serving as a sound element. An early account associates it with birth and nurture; today it commonly means “written character.”

components.text: The roof element sets the indoor scene in the traditional interpretation.
The child appears in the traditional scene; the account also assigns 子 a sound role.

takeaway.text: The proposed link from birth and nurture to “written character” is an old explanation, but its development and chronology remain unresolved.

relationships.text: In the traditional construction, 宀 depicts the roof or indoor setting in the proposed child-under-a-roof scene.
In the traditional construction, 子 depicts the child beneath the roof.

The traditional account assigns 子 a sound role. The reported Old Chinese comparison gives compatible consonant correspondences, though the exact dataset entries were not independently verified upstream; current Mandarin 子 zǐ and 字 zì are also comparable but do not establish the ancient relation.
